body: Thailand uses large, white licence plates for passenger vehicles and yellow ones for commercial vehicles. Yellow commercial plates are unique to Thailand in Southeast Asia, but be careful not to confuse them with the yellow plates for regular vehicles in Laos.
Thailand drives on the left-hand side of the road. This is a key differentiator from its neighbors, Cambodia and Laos, which drive on the right.
The Thai bollard is square-shaped with a pointed top and has black-and-white stripes. Similar bollards can also be found in Cambodia, Laos, and Indonesia.
Signposts in Thailand are uniquely square and bulky, usually white, and often have the bottom painted black. This design is exclusive to Thailand within Southeast Asia.
Concrete roads with a large, square-shaped pattern are common in Thailand. This feature is also frequently seen in the Philippines and less often in Indonesia.
Thailand uses square concrete poles with small vertical holes running up them. Similar poles are found in Sri Lanka, Cambodia, and Laos, so other clues are necessary for a definitive guess.

The Thai script is compact and often features tiny circles within its letters. It is very similar to the Lao script, so checking the driving side is important to differentiate between the two countries.
Thailand uses yellow middle lines, which can be either solid or dashed. This contrasts with Malaysia, which only uses white middle lines.
Street light poles in Thailand often have red-and-black or black-and-white stripes at the bottom.
Thailand is known for its very distinct long, thin lamp posts that hang out over the side of the road.
Directional signs on smaller roads are white and composed of two parts, sometimes featuring a Garuda emblem. Highway signs are green and often include place names in both Thai and Latin script.

Thai road markers often feature a Garuda emblem, which can be either white or black. White Garudas indicate country roads, while black Garudas signify province roads, corresponding to different map colors.
Besides the national flag, it is common to see royal flags, which are usually yellow, lining the streets in Thailand.
Distinctive small green signs are found all around Thailand, especially in villages, and are unique to the country.

Most Generation 3 coverage in Thailand has no visible car, similar to Vientiane in Laos and some areas in Cambodia. Rarely, you might encounter coverage from a bike trekker or a white car with a visible brake light.
Provincial road signs and waystones in Thailand often display a two-letter abbreviation of the province name in Thai script. These abbreviations are not used for national roads.

Black boxes on utility poles often provide a three-letter abbreviation for the province, which can be useful for region-guessing. Two common formats are used, often starting with the abbreviation or with 'TCC-L2'.
The far south of Thailand has a large Muslim population. In these areas, you are more likely to see mosques, Islamic attire, and the Jawi script on signs.
Thailand has two relatively flat and dry regions, one north of Bangkok and another to the east. The eastern area can feel slightly drier.
Tall mountains are most commonly found in northwestern Thailand. The southern peninsula also has some mountainous areas.
The centre-north of Thailand is characterized by low, smooth, and forested mountains.
Steep mountains with significant exposed rock are most common in the west and on the southern peninsula.
While red soil can be found throughout Thailand, it is most common in the northeast.
Gravel roads are found throughout Thailand but are particularly common in the north, northeast, and parts of the western border.
Rubber wood plantations are common in Thailand, with most being located in the south. They are recognizable by the small, black taps on the tree trunks.
The majority of Thailand’s rice cultivation occurs in the central plains around Bangkok and in the northeast.
Rice cultivated during the dry season is most common in the central plains. Dry season coverage often has a noticeable haze in the sky.
During the wet season, the majority of Thailand's rice cultivation takes place in the eastern plains.
Since over 90% of Thailand's palm oil is produced in the south, large palm plantations are a very strong clue for being in southern Thailand.
Dense plantations of short or medium-sized coconut palms are a good indicator for being in the area west of Bangkok.
Plantations of tall coconut palms are most common in the Prachuap Khiri Khan province on the peninsula.
Large numbers of palmyra palms are most common on the eastern coast of the peninsula, particularly south of Bangkok and in the far south.
Areca palms are found across the peninsula but are especially common around the province of Ranong.
Sugar cane cultivation is most prevalent in central and eastern Thailand.
Cassava, a bush-like plant with digitate leaves, is found throughout Thailand but is most common in the central and northeastern plains.
Corn is most commonly cultivated in the north and central regions of Thailand.
Extensive fruit plantations are concentrated in the valley between Chiang Mai and Lamphun in the north, and in the eastern provinces of Sa Kaeo and Chanthaburi.
Durian plantations are most common around Chanthaburi. Young trees are cone-shaped, while mature trees have dark bark and low-hanging branches.
Pineapple plantations are most commonly found to the southeast and southwest of Bangkok.
Dense eucalyptus plantations are most common around the eastern province of Sa Kaeo.
Teak trees (Tectona grandis), known for their large leaves and yellow flowers, are found in high densities in the north.
Pine trees (specifically Tenasserim pines) are almost exclusively found in the north and northwest of Thailand.
Garden croton, a decorative plant with colorful leaves, is most common around Ranong and other coastal provinces.
Gray corrugated metal roofs are most common in the north and south of Thailand, though they can appear anywhere.
Regular utility poles with a Chilean-style indent are found around Bangkok. Larger, thicker versions of these poles can be found on highways throughout the country.
Wind turbines are concentrated in specific areas: west of Chaiyaphum and Nakhon Ratchasima, and on the eastern coast of Songkhla and Nakhon Si Thammarat.
A specific black bollard with three large white reflectors is most frequently seen in the northern provinces of Chiang Mai and Mae Hong Son.

Insulators with 7 or more ridges are a good clue for the southern half of the peninsula or highways in the far northern provinces of Chiang Rai and Phayao. The standard for the rest of the country is 5 or 6 ridges.
On the southern peninsula, from Ranong and Chumphon southwards, utility poles often have only one insulator on the crossbar.
Conversely, poles with two insulators on the crossbar are found in the rest of Thailand (north of Ranong and Chumphon).
The island of Phuket is very touristy and wealthy, characterized by modern buildings, resorts, heavy traffic, and a hilly landscape.
